transcript.text: hi, we keep losing customers every month and i dont know what to do about it

That sounds frustrating, and it's good that you're looking at it. So I understand your situation: customers are leaving every month, and you'd like to slow that down. Can you tell me a bit about your business and what "losing a customer" looks like in practice? For example, do they cancel a subscription, or do they just stop buying?

We run a home internet company in Manchester. About 9,000 customers. They cancel their contract, usually with a month's notice. Roughly 3 in every 100 leave each month. I don't really know why they go.

Thanks, that helps. You have about 9,000 customers, roughly 3 in every 100 cancel each month, and you'd like to understand why and slow it down. Suppose you did know why. What would you be able to do about it? You might reach out to customers who look likely to leave, fix something in the service, or change pricing. Who in the business would act on it?

Mostly my customer care team. They ring people up. They can get through about 300 calls a month, that's about all they have time for. So really I want to know who to ring first, the ones most likely to go.

That's clear, thank you. So what you need is a ranked list: each month, the 300 customers your care team should ring first because they look most likely to cancel. The "why" would be a useful extra, but the list comes first. Do you have a customer table you can share with us? Ideally it would show who has cancelled in the past, plus whatever you know about each customer, such as their plan, how long they've been with you, what they pay, or whether they've contacted support.

Yeah, I think so. We have a billing system and I can get an export into Excel. It's got customer number, start date, plan, monthly bill, how many support calls they've made, and whether they've left. I haven't sent it yet. Is that enough to go on, or do you need something else?

Yes, that's a good start. Customer number, start date, plan, monthly bill, support calls and whether they've left are enough to build a first ranking of who to ring. Please send the Excel export when you can. One thing to check in it first. For the people who left, does the file show the date they left, or only a yes/no that they've gone? And do you know if the support-call count is the total up to today, or up to the point they gave notice?

Not sure, to be honest. I'd have to ask whoever runs the billing system. I think it just shows whether they've gone, not when. I don't know about the support calls, whether it stops at notice or goes up to today.

That's fine. You don't need to know yet. Those two questions are for whoever runs your billing system, and I'll come back to them. The reason they matter is this. If the call count runs up to today, customers who have already left will look like heavy callers, because many ring to cancel. A ranking built on that would look sharp on past data but do worse on the customers you still have. You can go two ways. One is to build the ranked list of 300 now. The other is to start by looking at who has left and what they have in common. Which would you like to do?

transcript.text: Hi! Could you pull which customers spent less this quarter than last quarter? I'm thinking of sending them something to bring them back, maybe a 15% coupon. The sales export is attached. [shares sales.csv]

Thanks, that's clear. You want the customers whose spend dropped from last quarter to this one, so you can send them a win-back offer like the 15% coupon. Your export has 2,020 orders (paid, refunded and cancelled), so I can build that list. Before I do, who do you picture getting the coupon? Should it go to anyone whose spend dipped even slightly, or mainly to customers who dropped a lot or stopped buying altogether?

Mainly the customers who are slipping but haven't fully stopped. I'd rather target someone who bought a lot last year and dropped sharply but still orders, than someone who bought once in 2025 and has been gone for months. I'm not sure where 'stopped buying' should start, so I'd like you to suggest a cutoff. I can only send 1,000 coupons, so if more customers qualify than that, I need them ranked rather than a yes/no list. I'd also like to leave out people whose spend barely moved, because they'd probably buy anyway and that's where coupons get wasted. Please count only paid orders. The table also has refunded and cancelled orders, and those shouldn't count as spend. The send date is the 15th and my manager approves the final list, so each customer should have a short reason for being on it. Before you build anything, can you tell me how you'd define the groups?

Here's how I'd define the groups. It's a starting point, and I'd test every cutoff against your data before locking it in. **What counts as spend:** paid orders only, added up per customer per quarter. That leaves out the 188 refunded and 99 cancelled orders. **The groups, comparing last quarter to this one:**
- **Slipping (the coupon list):** the customer spent last quarter, has at least one paid order this quarter, and this quarter's spend is clearly lower. As a first cut I'd say down by about a third or more. I'd look at how drops are spread across your customers before fixing that number. - **Stopped (left out):** no paid order for a stretch of time. I'd set that stretch from how long your customers normally wait between orders, so it's based on your data rather than a round number. A customer who bought once in 2025 and has been gone for months lands here, not on the list. - **Steady (left out):** spend barely moved, up or down. Those are the people who would probably buy anyway. - **Growing or new (left out):** spend went up, or they only started this quarter. **Ranking and reasons:** if more than 1,000 customers are slipping, I'd rank them by how much they bought over the past year and how sharply they dropped. That puts the big buyers who are falling off at the top. Each customer would get a one-line reason your manager can check. It would give last quarter's spend, this quarter's spend, the days since their last paid order, and their spend over the past year. **What the export covers:** it starts at the very beginning of January 2025 and runs into March. If this quarter isn't finished, everyone will look like they dropped, so the comparison could mislead. Is "this quarter" January to March of this year, and was the export pulled at the end of the quarter or part way through it?

Yes, 'this quarter' is January to March 2026, and 'last quarter' is October to December 2025. The table runs from 2025 into Q1 2026. I'm not sure when the export was pulled, though, so I can't say whether March is complete. I'll check the latest order_date in the file myself. If March looks partial, please use the last full date in the data as the end of the window and tell me that's what you did. Before you build the list, please show me how many customers fall into each group (slipping, stopped, steady, growing/new) and the gap-based cutoff you picked for 'stopped', so I can see how the numbers move if the cutoff changes. I'd also like the logic written as steps I can rerun in Excel or a pivot, because the manager will ask how the list was made, and I'd rather be able to explain it than just hand over a result.

I checked the window, but I don't have your group counts or the "stopped" cutoff yet. Those come next. - **Dates:** `order_date` is stored as text, but all 2,020 rows convert to proper dates, so nothing is lost. - **March looks complete:** The file has 120 orders dated in March, against 128 in February. The last few days of March still show orders at about the same pace as the rest of the month, so the data doesn't tail off. I'd use the full quarter, January to March 2026. - **A few orders are dated after March:** A very small number are dated April or later. The tool hides groups that small, so I can't give you the exact latest date. It suggests the export was pulled after the quarter closed. I'd leave those orders out of both quarters, since they fall outside the window. You may want to look at them when you check the latest `order_date`. - **Spend:** It counts the 1,733 paid orders, from 938 customers. The 188 refunded and 99 cancelled orders stay out, as you asked. Next I'll count customers in each group (slipping, stopped, steady, growing/new). I'll show the numbers at a few "stopped" cutoffs, so you can see how they move. The cutoff will come from the gaps between your customers' own orders. I'll also write the logic as numbered steps you can rerun in Excel or a pivot. One thing changes the "stopped" counts. Happy to. I've had a first look at sales.csv. It has 2,020 orders, each with a date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer. Most orders are paid (1,733). 188 were refunded and 99 were cancelled, so there's plenty to dig into. To point this at something useful to you, what's on your mind about the business right now? It could be a decision coming up, something that feels off, or something you'd like to grow.
I want to start a loyalty programme in March. I need to know what kinds of customers I have, I guess. Like who buys a lot and who doesn't. Not sure how to split them up though.

Thanks, that helps. So you're launching a loyalty programme in March and want to see who your customers are before you design it. One thing I can see already: your table has about 1,002 different customers across 2,020 orders, so roughly two orders each on average. That means there's likely a big group who've bought only once or twice, and a smaller group who buy a lot. What do you most want the programme to do: reward your best customers, get occasional buyers to come back more often, or win back people who've drifted away?

Honestly, a bit of everything I guess. The regulars should feel looked after, and I want the people who only come once to come back. I don't really know about the ones who left. Whatever you find, I need to be able to explain it to my store managers in December, so keep it simple.

Here's what I took from you: you want the regulars to feel looked after and the one-time buyers to come back. You're not sure about the lapsed ones. You also have to explain the result to your store managers in December, so it needs to be simple. For the groups, I'd count only paid orders as real purchases. Refunded and cancelled orders would be set aside. Tell me if you'd rather count them. I've put three ways forward below. I'd start with the first one, because its groups are easy to explain to managers. It also shows how big the "came once" and "drifted away" groups are, so you can decide whether the lapsed group is worth targeting at all.

choices.what: Sort every customer into a few plain groups using how many paid orders they have and how recently they last bought (for example: one-time buyers, occasional, regulars, drifted away), using customer_id, order_date, amount and status. You get: For each group: how many customers, how much they spend, and their share of your sales. Each group is described in one sentence a store manager can repeat. Trade-off: The cut-offs (like 'regular = 4+ orders') are a judgement call we agree together, not something the data discovers. Effort: Quick: numbers back in one pass, then we adjust the cut-offs if needed.

choices.title: Let the data find the groups
choices.what: DCLab looks at how often, how recently and how much each customer buys, and finds the natural groupings itself. You get: A set of customer groups with a profile of each, which may show patterns you would not have thought to look for. Trade-off: Harder to explain to managers, since the groups come from the maths rather than a rule. With about two orders per customer, the groups may also not be very distinct. Effort: A bit longer: a project is built and then checked with you before you rely on it.

choices.title: Loyalty programme brief for March
choices.what: A short written recommendation on how to design the programme for regulars, one-time buyers and lapsed customers, based on what your sales data shows. You get: A plain-language plan you can walk your store managers through in December. Trade-off: Less detail on the customer groups themselves. It leans on a first pass over the data rather than a full breakdown. Effort: Moderate: one written brief.

I'm thinking about hiring someone to look after the company members. I'm not sure it's worth the money. I need to decide by end of November. I have a list of members in a spreadsheet from our booking system, but I haven't looked at it much.

Thanks, that helps a lot. If you picture the hire working out well, what would it have done: kept company members from leaving, got them to book or spend more, or something else? Whenever you're ready, please also share the spreadsheet so I can see what it holds.
Mostly that they stay longer and complain less. I'm not sure about spending more, to be honest. I'll look for the spreadsheet and send it when I've found it.

Thanks, that's clear: you want to know if company members stay longer and complain less than regular ones, because that's what a hire would be paid to improve. Take your time finding the spreadsheet. So you want to rank your destinations by how much money they bring in, and cut the three at the bottom. I looked at the table. It has five real destinations (Paris, Bangkok, Dubai, London and Istanbul) and a "TEST" destination with 12 bookings, which looks like leftover test data. Cutting three real ones would leave you with two. Cancellations also differ by destination: Paris and Istanbul lose the fewest bookings, and Dubai loses the most. The table has a price on each booking but no cost column. When you say "make the most money", do you mean the revenue you keep after cancellations, or the profit after what each destination costs you to run? If it's profit, do you have costs somewhere?

Use the price on each booking as what we earn. I don't know the costs off the top of my head. Why only five places? I offer about 20 destinations, so I thought the file had all of them. I need the bottom 3 soon, the catalogue goes to print in 3 weeks.

The file only has five real destinations, and I can't tell from it why. It holds 1,500 bookings across all three channels (web, app and agent), so it isn't missing a whole sales channel. The five are Paris, Bangkok, Dubai, London and Istanbul, and each has a similar number of bookings. The 12 TEST rows are the only other destination. This matters for your decision. If I ranked these five and named the bottom three, I'd be picking the weakest of five, not of your 20. Your real bottom three could be among the destinations I can't see. Do you know how you pulled this file? Was there a filter, a date range or a sample, or does your booking system keep the other destinations somewhere else, such as another export or another tool?

I'm not sure how the file was pulled. I'm not technical, so I don't know about filters or date ranges. I need all 20 destinations, and the catalogue goes to print in 3 weeks. Tell me in plain words how to get the full list, or what to check in my booking system.

- **Destination:** it should say "All", not a short list. - **Dates:** it should cover at least the last 12 months. A shorter range can make some destinations look weaker only because of the season. - **Sales channel:** web, app and agent should all be included. They already are in this file. - **Status:** it should include cancelled bookings as well as confirmed ones. **2. Check whether your bookings live in more than one place.** Some businesses keep other regions or suppliers in a separate system, or a partner portal. If the other destinations are somewhere else, that explains the five. **3. If you can't find it, ask the person who sent you the file or set up the system.** You could send them this:

> "Can you export every booking, for all destinations, for the last 12 months, including cancelled ones? Please include the booking date, travel date, destination, channel, price and whether it was cancelled. The file I have only shows 5 destinations and I need all of them."

**4. Check the new file when it arrives.** Count the different destinations. You should get about 20. Send me the new file and I'll rank all your destinations by the money you keep after cancellations. I'll also clean up the price column and leave out the TEST rows. Do you know who sent you this file, or who looks after your booking system?

I can't give you a trustworthy bottom 3 by money kept today, for two reasons. - **The price column is stored as text, not numbers.** It has 1,126 different values and may mix currency symbols. What the file does show is cancellations. The gaps are modest, and cancellations alone don't tell you the money. Here is what I'd do today. Ask your team one question: "Is there another export or another system with bookings for our other destinations?" Meanwhile I can prepare the price column and leave out the TEST rows. Your ranking would then be ready to run as soon as the full file arrives. To clean the price properly, I need to know one thing. Are all your prices in one currency, or do you sell in a mix, for example euros and dollars?

I'm not sure about the currency. I think we sell in one currency, but I don't know which, and my team would know. I need to decide in 3 weeks, so tell me plainly what you can do with this file today, in a few short lines.

- Take out the 12 TEST rows, which leaves 1,488 bookings. - Turn the price text into numbers, so the file is ready to rank. - Compare your 5 real destinations on cancellations, with free cancellation and sales channel as extra detail. **I can't:**
- Name your bottom 3. This file holds 5 of your roughly 20 destinations, so any bottom 3 from it could be wrong. - Add up money kept until your team confirms the currency. If prices are in more than one currency, a total would be wrong. **Two questions for your team:**
1. Where are the bookings for the other destinations? 2. What currency do you sell in? With both answers and the full file, I can rank all your destinations and name the bottom 3 well before print. Do you want me to get this file ready now, so the ranking can run as soon as the full export arrives?
Yes, get the file ready now. I'll ask my team about the other 15 destinations and the currency. Meanwhile, show me the 5 destinations ranked by cancellations so I can see what you can do today.

I've started getting the file ready. First step: remove the 12 TEST rows. That's a small cut, so it didn't need an extra yes from you. Next, I'll turn the price text into numbers. I'll leave the currency question open until your team answers, so I won't add up any money yet. **Your 5 destinations, ranked by cancellations, most cancelled first:**

2. London
3. Bangkok
4. Istanbul
5. Paris

London and Bangkok are almost tied. Dubai loses the most bookings, and Paris and Istanbul lose the fewest. I can send the exact cancellation rates and booking counts as a table if you want them. transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your headline number, and show your 3% base rate next to it. **Why PR-AUC**
- ROC-AUC can look very good when positives are rare. Its false-positive rate is divided by the huge pool of non-churners. A model can therefore post an impressive ROC-AUC while most of the customers it flags don't churn. - PR-AUC tracks what your manager cares about. Of the customers the model flags, how many really leave (precision)? And how many of the leavers does it catch (recall)? - PR-AUC has a built-in reference point. A model with no skill scores about the base rate, which for you is the 3% of customers who churn. So you can say "the model's PR-AUC is X, against a no-skill baseline equal to our churn rate." A manager can follow that without any statistics. **Caveats**
- PR-AUC depends on the base rate. Don't compare it with numbers from a dataset or period with a different churn rate. - ROC-AUC is still a fair measure of how well the model ranks customers. Include it as a secondary line if someone asks. - Managers usually respond best to a concrete statement. For example: "If we contact the top slice of customers by risk, this share of them churn, and we reach this share of all churners." Choose the size of that slice to match how many customers your retention team can actually contact. Use average precision (`average_precision_score` in scikit-learn) for PR-AUC. It is more honest than a trapezoid-interpolated area, which can be too optimistic. If you'd like, I can help you word this for your manager. If you later want the numbers worked out on your own table, share it and we can do that.
Got it, that's the reasoning I needed. Can you give me the one-line version for the slide, with the 3% baseline in it?

Here's a one-liner for the slide:

> **PR-AUC of [your model's value], against a 3% no-skill baseline (our churn rate).**

If you want to show the lift too, you can add: "That is [PR-AUC ÷ baseline] times better than chance at finding churners." Fill that bracket in with your own result. A shorter version, if space is tight:

> **PR-AUC: [your value] (baseline: 3%)**

Does that wording work for your slide? Or would you like a version that also says how many churners you'd catch by contacting the top slice of customers by risk?
That works, thanks. Skip the lift line. Give me the top-slice version in one line and I'm done.

Here's the top-slice line:

> **Contacting the top [X]% of customers by predicted risk would reach [Y]% of all churners, and [Z]% of the people contacted would actually churn (vs. 3% overall).**

Pick X to match how many customers your retention team can contact. Then fill in Y (recall) and Z (precision) from your model's results at that cutoff. Good luck with the slide!

after.title: A first look at your own no-show numbers
after.what: Once the export arrives, DCLab counts how often appointments end in a no-show and when it happens: by day, time, how far ahead the visit was booked, and a patient's earlier misses. If reminder texts are in the file, it also compares patients who got one with those who didn't.
after.gets: Real numbers on your no-shows, and a clear view of whether misses are concentrated enough that a simple rule, like phoning patients who have missed before, would do most of the job.
after.tradeoff: It describes what already happened. It doesn't flag who will miss next week.
after.effort: Light. It needs only the export, and the receptionist's check this afternoon.

after.title: A model that flags likely no-shows ahead of time
after.what: DCLab builds a prediction from your two years of appointments, tested on appointments it hasn't seen, so you learn whether no-shows are predictable and how well. The output would be a short list of upcoming appointments to phone or double-book.
after.gets: An honest answer to real or hype for your practice, and a short daily list the receptionist could act on.
after.tradeoff: With only a handful of no-shows a week, the history may be thin, and the model may not beat a simple rule. It needs a clear no-show status in the data, and I'd only build it after you say yes.
after.effort: Moderate. It builds on the first look, and I'd suggest doing that first.

after.title: Plain guidance first: what to share and whether this is worth it
after.what: No data work yet. I'd explain what to leave out of the export, how to think about texts versus phoning versus prediction for a practice your size, and how to judge the few-thousand-dollar question.
after.gets: A clear checklist for this afternoon, and a way to judge the spend before you commit.
after.tradeoff: It gives guidance, not numbers from your own appointments.
after.effort: Very light. It's a conversation, with no export needed.
